findings.message: The success criteria explicitly promises that the update transaction handles 'the local-edits cases — with no manual git surgery'. However, Phase 4's update transaction preflight step 2 handles local edits by refusing the update entirely and printing copy-paste git commands (`git stash`, `git checkout`, etc.) for the user to execute manually, explicitly noting that a pop conflict is theirs to resolve. This is the exact definition of manual git surgery and directly violates the stated success criterion, creating a severely frustrating update UX for any collaborator who tweaks a shipped file.

findings.criterion: (4) agent trio behaves identically to the author's
findings.message: The Windows per-OS durability contract mandates a 15-second blocking retry loop for AV locks, followed by a loud crash if the lock persists. From a UX perspective, freezing the agent for up to 15 seconds on a routine file save and then failing the operation entirely is highly disruptive. If AV locks are common enough to require this backoff, shifting the burden to the user to manually configure OS-level AV exclusions creates significant runtime friction and violates the 'works-on-arrival' expectation.

The exposure matrix allows non-loopback LAN exposure but strictly requires TLS ('TLS or refuse'). However, Phase 3 explicitly defers TLS certificate provisioning automation, leaving only a 'documented manual path'. Forcing a collaborator to manually provision and configure TLS certificates just to safely access their instance from another machine on their local network is a massive UX hurdle that contradicts the 'zero-friction' intent of the security model.

The success criteria explicitly promises 'no manual git surgery', yet Phase 4 contradicts this by requiring the operator to manually execute `git stash`, run the update, perform `git stash pop`, and resolve any resulting merge conflicts themselves if they have local edits. This violates the premise of a low-friction package that a collaborator can easily run and maintain.

The first-contact integrity ceremony instructs the operator to 'verify the archive hash against the out-of-band value.' However, Phase 4 dictates distribution via a persistent git release branch. Because the operator is cloning a repository rather than downloading a monolithic release tarball, there is no 'archive' to hash. This makes the critical initial trust anchor technically impossible for the operator to execute.

The one-time pairing code for headless environments expires in 90 seconds. In a real-world operator scenario involving remote servers, establishing an SSH tunnel, switching machine contexts, opening a browser, and typing the code can easily exceed this limit, leading to frustrating timeouts during onboarding.

Phase 3 asserts the master token "never appears on any process argv" as a strict invariant. However, the interactive bootstrap "opens the browser exactly once with the token in the URL FRAGMENT". Opening a browser via standard OS mechanisms (like xdg-open, open, or invoking the browser executable directly) requires passing the full URL as a command-line argument. This places the master token directly onto the process argv of the spawner or browser, directly violating the invariant and exposing the token to any local user able to inspect process lists (e.g., via ps or WMI).

Phase 3 states the headless pairing code is "per-IP attempt rate-limited." However, the success criteria dictate the instance operates "behind a loopback reverse proxy". If the rate limiter relies on the incoming network connection IP, all requests will appear to come from the proxy's IP (127.0.0.1). Unless the application is strictly configured to securely parse proxy headers (like X-Forwarded-For) without being vulnerable to spoofing from direct loopback connections, the rate limit will apply globally to the proxy. This breaks the per-IP defense and enables a trivial denial-of-service, locking out the pairing endpoint after 3 total attempts by anyone.

Phase 6 mandates removing the status-request text from agent prompts while the engine injects the status block directly into the transcript. If the agent's system prompt contains no instructions explaining the purpose and origin of the injected status block, the LLM will encounter unexplained, ungrounded data in its history. This degrades its context understanding and violates the North Star's "honesty" criterion (NS5) by introducing unverified context. Furthermore, removing these instructions from the prompts constitutes modifying the skills themselves, contradicting the explicitly stated non-goal of not "re-architecting trio/foundry skills' internals."
